Hi all,
hope to not beat a dead horse with this, i did a little search
on the group but i found nothing about it.

What do you think about the idea of making the Silence
of Death format official (both for standard constructed and limited event)
in the VEKN rules ?

I discussed this in my playgroup, and all of us agreed that
this format could help a lot in getting new players introduced
into the game at official tournaments, because the SoD spares the

> of Death format official (both for standard constructed and limited event)
> in the VEKN rules ?

it kills one of the best features of the game, namely table talk, so making
the format official would be a bad thing.
I had "co-designed" the format with Stephane Lavrut (nothing to brag about,
really, my point is that I'm familiar with the format). The original and
simple idea is that it makes games quicker (actually, the idea came up when
the shop was like due to close within the hour, so we couldn't afford the
usual long discussions) in average. The second (and last) benefit is that it
attracts the pool of players who either are not good at deal-making or hate
it (or both), and who therefore shun the regular sanctioned tournaments. If
you happen to host sanctioned tournaments on a regular basis (i.e. 1/month),
it can be nice for unsanctioned tournaments, just for the sake of a little
change here and then, but that's the end of it.

Stone

Frankly, the point about newbie/less-experienced players shouldn't be an
issue. When new players come to give a try to VtES in a shop, I'm ok to play
with them, so long as it's a 3-player game. In a 5-player game, it's just
not possible to play properly, because the newbie is manipulated by the rest
of the table and takes too much time trying to grasp what the gazillion
cards mean. Once the newbie is a bit familiar with the game, the rest (i.e.
deal-making) just comes naturally. Even more, they learn a lot from
experienced table talk, without doing anything : in our last game with a new
player, the newbie was in bad shape due to his inexperience (all vamps in
torpor, 3 pool). The other four started ripping each other's throat and it
ended with the newbie getting cross-table rescue and the like, getting a way
better position than he could have dreamt of.
As for the false "newbies" that already have an experience of duel games
(LoR, WoW etc.), they're often good enough with TCG mechanisms and tactics
to just climb the learning curve in no time, and hop straight to deal
making.
Stone

great deal of time to do it) failed. All the rest of the game/games
involved "reasonable" levels of table talk and minimal quid-pro-quo
dealing ("rescue my guy from torpor and I'll help you pass your next

terms of deal making.

I think in the long run, my basic point is that the level of deal
making/table talk that I am familiar with on a grand scale is perfectly
reasonable is is unlikely to scare anyone off while any kind of deal
making/table talk that would scare someone off is something that
shouldn't be going on anyway (as the PTW, anti-collusion, and "all deals
are off when you get to 2 players" tournament rules exist to attempt to
curtail).

-Play to Win: A great deal of significant deal making comes specifically
at the expense of one's ability to win, based on someone pre-emptively
deciding that they can't win, so they give up their ability to win in
the name of the losing end of a deal, justifying it by saying "I
couldn't win anyway". Deals like this tend to benefit one player by
another player arbitrarily deciding to not play to win.

-All Deals are Off in the End Game: A great deal of significant deal
making comes down to one player helping another player win which, in
theory, should not happen, and this rule is an ironclad example of an
attempt to curtail such activity. In practice, this rule is virtually
meaningless (as you can accept the losing end of a deal when there are 3
players, and when you get to 2 players, due to you helping someone else
get into a stronger position, the likelyhood of the "losing end" player
being able to now oust the "winning end" player is pretty low).

-Play in a Timely Fashion: Any kind of deal making that is excessively
long (i.e. the kind of table talk that scares people away from the game)
is not playing in a timely fashion, and should be called on for delay of
game. Especially in a game with a 2 hour time limit.

deal making come from the people who are losing, and generally don't
make them win--they make the losing player lose a bit less and make
someone else win. As the goal of the game is to win the game, not just
lose less, people shouldn't be making deals that make them lose less
while making someone else win. As that is not playing to win.

> under a certain set of rules (actual one), will make them to lessen their

that is likely to scare folks away from the game. And you don't need to
force or pursuade anyone to do anything. Just don't enable them.

> The rules does not specify a given quantity, afaik, i'm sorry.

The rules on timely game play and delay of game specify that people play
in a timely fashion and not delay the game. Talking a lot is delaying
the game.

Hi folks,

Surely excessive deal making slowing down the game to the point it's
going to time out is a completely separate issue from table talk
scaring away new players. Experienced players may spend more time
dealing, but less experienced players also spend more time asking
questions. There seems to be a big assumption here that events in
which new players can be encouraged to learn the game must be
sanctioned tournaments in which experienced players will wish to win
for the sake of their ratings.

If you want to learn football, you don't put a team together from your
friends who've never played before and expect to be able to compete in
a major league.

Assuming you don't have some friendly regular meetings in the area
newbies can go along to, the simplest and most obvious solution in my
eyes is to run "newbie events" which encourage new players to take
part without encouraging experienced players to come along and destroy
them with their powerful decks of doom. If your local players are
unwilling to turn up to such things, I appreciate you would have to
rely on other means (i.e. material rewards) to encourage them or you
could simply be glad they're not around to dispirit the newbies.

Let's face it, nobody enjoys trying a new game and being trounced by a
group of experienced players who give you no chance. In a tournament
environment, that is precisely what new players can expect, and
rightly so. Hence the solution is not to change tournament rules for
the experienced players, but to target newbies with a separate and
less-competitive event.

I agree, but I see a contradiction in the existing "Slow Play" rules

Currently, if a player wants to 'activate' the slow play rule, there's
two ways to do it. You can interrupt the conversation and ask folks
to move along, or you can call over a judge and complain. This system
works great in games like Scrabble, where whether or not your opponent
likes you is 100% irrelevant to the gameplay.

But VTES isn't like that. Not by a long-shot.

There's a social consequence to "calling the cops" on other players
for playing slow. Everyone reacts differently to it. Some people
*like* acts of social aggression like that, and will shift their
faction allegiance based on it. Some people get resentful, and take
revenge on you later for calling them out. Some people don't even
notice. Some people shut down, as if their dad had just yelled at
them. It's tough to know what the result is going to be.

These real-world consequences change the social dynamics of the game
being played. If your cross-table buddy is playing slow, none of the
other players are being willing to call the cops, and you know that
he's a grumpy fellow who gets mad when the Slow Play rule is called,
as a player you are put in a very strange position. Either you can
let him continue to be rude, and keep his (flimsy) alliance, or you
can call him out and potentially make a cross-table enemy. How does
one play to win in this scenario?

The political nature of VTES means that when players are being slow,
requiring the players to speak out to point out possible delays means
that double-binds often emerge that are, in my opinion, inappropriate
in this game. I may be missing the boat here, but that's the
contradiction I see in the existing Slow Play rule.

If this is true (and I'm not saying I'm sure that it is), what would a
solution look like? I'm not sure, but I *can* think of ways to soften
this effect.

At the next event I hold, I intend to experiment with something like
the following system:

1) Each player will be given a "boredom indicator". I'll
probably use little flags, or Warhammer vampire counts, or something.
Something visible from a judge's level.

2) Any player can, at any time, move their boredom indicator in
front of their spread (for best effect, this will be done with eye
rolling and muffled groans, to reinforce the message). This indicates
that player is officially bored, and wants the discussion to move on,
but lacks the "excuse me, but can we move along here?" factor.

3) If 2 or more players express their boredom in this way, the
other players will be obligated to begin to wrap up their discussion.
If, after a reasonable amount of time (say 2-3 minutes) they do not
wrap it up, the judge may choose to begin to exact penalties.

This is not a change in the rules. It's simply a more gentle way for
players to communicate the current game state (no flags = "not
delayed", 1 flag = "becoming delayed", 2 flags = "delayed").

I'm sure there are ways to use this as a "mafia" mechanic, to try to
force people to not make deals at all, but that's why the penalties
ultimately have to fall to the judge.

Am I on crack?

-Jason

It is if it is keeping other people from playing the game. Two people
having an earnest discussion of how they can best split the table that
prevents three other people from taking actions for a long period of
time is certainly disruptive. A tournament round has 2 hours in it. In
a 5 player game, that gives each player about 24 minutes of play time.

players B and C by actions that are arguably unecessary, that is bad.

Spending a long time actually playing the game (taking actions,
playing cards) is always acceptable, given that it is done is a
reasonably timely fashion. Spending a long time talking about playing
the game, during the game, is not always going to be. For my money.

inevitable in any multi-player game (even though the rulebook does not
recognize it at all). But at a certain point, table talk can, even if
done in earnest, cross from reasonable to disruptive. And if it is
scaring people away from the game (as per the original discussion), it
may very well have crossed that point.

Or, alternatively, 'actively' playing vs. 'passively' playing.

For the real life reduction ad absurdum that this distinction can lead
to, see the CCG version of Illuminati. The demise of that game came,
in part, from the fact that a player wishing to do so could construct
a deck capable of winning the game on the first turn of play. If that
player went first, then he would be the only 'active' participant in
the game at all. Which seems like a pretty big problem for game
'play', though, in that case, the 'active' player is actually
'playing' using the rules, cards, etc. and not 'deal-making' or
'negotiating' or 'meditating on strategic issues' or otherwise
engaging in other 'rules-neutral' activities. (By 'rules-neutral' I
mean 'neither allowed nor disallowed by the rules'.)

Which is to say that Peter (and Emiliano have) a point. If permitted
play styles are regularly and predictably destroying a large subset of
players' enjoyment of the game, it is not good for the game. (Well,
unless the same is also attracting a similar amount of new players, I
suppose.) OTOH, I don't think anyone (except maybe Emiliano) is
arguing that V:TES has reached this point.

Alex

state change, and removes 17% of the table's total available time to
accomplish in-game objectives. Even the example of resolving 20+ block-
combats takes less time, and the game state is constantly changing
throughout the string of actions. Deal-making is (can be) uniquely and
disproportionately time consuming, in a game with time limits.

easily exploited. Anyone can make better decisions when they stop to think

earnest contemplation one can make, and, for me anyways, more consideration

minutes per turn once the mid-game is reached (by about turn 4-6, things

fully. What fun.

to attend. If somebody is *learning* the game, they should be allowed
to bend rules when they make mistakes (take back cards they didnt
realise they couldnt play, etc) - it's a learning environment, and it
doesn't matter. If they're at a level where restrictions need to be
applied to the rules or they stop playing, then they're clearly not
ready for tournament play yet.

deliberately act in a way that has been seen to be putting new players

talk is too off-putting for new players, have a non-sanctioned event
which limits it. If there's too many cards for your players, limit it
to just 3rd Ed precons or something. If the mechanics are confusing
people, limit it to standard bleed/politics/combat with no "trick"
decks, or hell, you could even ban political actions. Whatever you
feel works to help people LEARN the game. There's nothing stopping you
doing that which I am aware of. But why must there be a single all-
encompassing official system for learning how to play? What comes
next? An official step-by-step order in which card texts must be
memorized? :p

If players aren't ready for tournaments, they don't need sanctioned

No, I'm really having a time more with wrapping my mind around what I
should be looking at for context, in terms of enforcement. Game state is
mostly useless, except as a gross metric for how complex the game state
is.
And again, what is fair in terms of one or two people consuming the
limited amount of time disproportionately.

> Deal-making time should not be curtailed just because one of the
> players at the table doesn't like it (just like you wouldn't keep
> someone from untapping all of her cards just because it takes 10x as
> long as someone else's untap phase). That is, playing the game is
> allowed.
>
> Excessive time used in any fashion (taking longer than necessary to
> conclude deal-making, analysis, or whatever) is already prohibited.

Even that statement changes the metric from time spent "in earnest", to
time spent that is "necessary", which IMO is a step in the right
direction. Although in a complex game situation, you can still claim
that a half-hour is necessary to fully discuss the aspects that factor
into a deal.

I'd rather that we still at least consider the possibility of a some
non-binding guidelines as to what is necessary and/or reasonable. Such
as, a "three-minute*" guide for the duration that the game state can
remain unaltered for the purpose of dialogue, and a "thirty second*"
guide for a single player's contemplation of the game state before
changing it. These could be extended by the Judge for mitigating
circumstances, but are (I think) useful for getting all players to make
their deals and consider their options without a disproportionate
consumption of the total time available for the round.

I know our international players won't like (and possibly won't
follow**) the analogy, but i see a lot of similarities to the VTES
judge's responsibilities, and that of a baseball umpire defining the
strike zone. But, the difference is that we have a lot less of a written
guide as to how to call balls and strikes. I don't think its a bad thing
to quantify judging a bit more than we have, so long as its understood to
be alterable at the discretion of the judge.

DZ
AW

*Please, pick some number more appropriate...

** for not-baseball fans abroad; in baseball, the strike zone is the area
over the width of home plate that reaches roughly from the bottom of the
batter's knees to the mid-torso (a horizontal line midway between the top
of the shoulders and the top of the uniform pants). A pitcher tries to
throw the ball into the strike zone three times, without the batter
hitting the ball into the field of play, in order to get the batter out.
Missing the strike zone four times allows the player to advance to first
base. In practice (but with limits), baseball umpires have discretion to
alter the strike zone (due to height of the batter, stance, etc.), much
in the same way that VTES Judges can use their discretion in assinging
different severity of penalties, and ruling on things like Play to Win
and Deal Legality, based on the particular circumstances of each
incident.
Baseball umpires have pretty extensive training and written guidelines,
to keep the strike zone consistent. Of course, there is always
controversy, game to game, but there is less variation in consistency
today than at many times in the past.

You know, I have thought more about this.

Perhaps if there was simply a different sanctioning label, say the Third
Tradition Tournaments, but all else was the same, it might not be that
tough.

Robyn would enter Archon's in the same as she does now. It would be
just as easy to enter a 3T Tournament as a limited tournament, although
I don't know if that is a big deal or not. Oscar/LSJ (don't know who it

spiff to have the rankings in the 3T Tourneys be posted on WW's site,

to move up - sort of like passing out of the Q circuit in PGA golf.

Silence of Death format, but regular VTES with deals and everything
else. The only difference is eligibility of players.

A player can play as long as their total number of tournaments played
ever is fewer than 10. The number can be tweaked, but you get the idea.

This means that those who are not very experienced can play in a
tournament level with others of their same level. After 10 tournies of
any type, you would then no longer be eligible to play in Third
Tradition sanctioned tourneys.

level of trust that players were not gaming the system by signing up for
new ID's just to play in what would be a "new player" tournament structure.

sanctioning. Archons would be the same, Robyn would enter them the
same. There would need to be a new ranking chart on WW's web site, but
